---
title: |
  Surprises in\
  time series analysis
author: Rob J Hyndman
date: 26 October 2026
url: robjhyndman.com/uconn2026
abstract: >-
  I will present a statistical framework for identifying anomalies in three time series settings: unusual observations within a single historical series, unusual series within a large collection, and real-time surveillance of incoming data streams.
  In each case, anomalies are identified using a probabilistic approach based on 'surprisal values' --- equal to minus the log (conditional) density of each observation --- with extreme value theory used to model the tail of the surprisal distribution and avoid strong parametric assumptions.
  The methods will be illustrated using the weird package for R, with examples including French and US mortality rates, and pharmaceutical sales.

## Surprisal probabilities

::: {.alertblock}
The probability of an observation at least as unlikely as $y_t$:

$$
  p_t = \mathbb{P}\big(f(Y) \le f(y_t)\big), \qquad Y \sim f
$$
:::

::: {.absolute .fragment top="300" left="740" width="480"}
::::: {.alertblock}
An observation is an **anomaly with respect to $f$** if $p_t < \alpha$.
:::::
:::

## Surprisals

::: {.alertblock}
The **surprisal** of an observation $y_t$ under density $f$ is $s_t = -\log f(y_t)$
:::

Surprisals are already familiar:

::: {.cards}
::::: {.block}
[Forecasting]{.block-title}

Log score for evaluating density forecasts
:::::

::::: {.block}
[Information theory]{.block-title}

Expected surprisal = entropy
:::::

::::: {.block}
[Likelihood]{.block-title}

Sum of surprisals = $-\log$&nbsp;likelihood
:::::
:::

## The surprisal distribution

Let $S = -\log f(Y)$ where $Y \sim f$, and $G(s) = \mathbb{P}(S \le s)$.
Then

$$
  p_t = \mathbb{P}(S \ge s_t) = 1 - G(s_t).
$$

An anomaly is an extreme value of the surprisal distribution.

::: {.cards .cards-2}
::::: {.block .fragment}
[$f$may be complicated]{.block-title}

Multimodal, multivariate or conditional: $G$ is still a univariate distribution on $\mathbb{R}$.
:::::

::::: {.alertblock .fragment}
[$f$may be wrong]{.block-title}

The [upper tail]{.alert} of $G$ can still be estimated using EVT.
:::::
:::

## Three-type theorem for surprisals

**A1: Sub-Gaussian**: $S = -\log f(Y)$ satisfies, for all $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and some $\nu > 0$, $\mathbb{E} \exp\{\lambda (S - \mathbb{E}[S])\} \le \exp\{\lambda^2 \nu^2/2\}$.

**A2: Sub-exponential**: $S$ is sub-exponential with parameters $\nu$ and $b$, i.e., $\mathbb{E} \exp\{\lambda(S - \mathbb{E}[S])\} \leq \exp\{\lambda^2\nu^2 / 2\}$ for all $|\lambda| < 1/b$.

**A3: Polynomial**: $|S|$ has polynomial moments of order $p \ge 1$; i.e., $\mathbb{E}[|S|^p] \le C^p$ for some $C > 0$ such that $C^p - 1 > 0$.

- A1 satisfied when $f$ has bounded support
- A2 satisfied when $\log f$ unbounded below, and light tails (e.g., Gaussian)
- A3 satisfied when $f$ has heavy tails (e.g., $t$ with df $\ge 3$)

## Three-type theorem for surprisals

Let $y_1,\dots,y_n$ be iid from density $f$, $s_t = -\log f(y_t)$, $M_n = \max\{s_1,\dots,s_n\}$, and $S = -\log f(Y)$ where $Y \sim f$.

1. Under A1:
   $$
     \sup_{s:s>0}\left| \mathbb{P}\left\{ \big|M_n - \mathbb{E}[S]\big| \ge \sqrt{2\nu^2 s}+\sqrt{2\nu^2\log(2n)} \right\} - e^{-s} \right|
     = o(1).
   $$
2. Under A2:
   $$
     \sup_{s:s>1/b}\left| \mathbb{P}\Big\{\big|M_n - \mathbb{E}[S]\big| \ge (2b)s + (2b)\log(2n)\Big\} - e^{-e^{-s}} \right|
     = o(1).
   $$
3. Under A3:
   $$
     \sup_{s:s>C}\left| \mathbb{P}\Big\{\big|M_n - \mathbb{E}[S]\big| \ge (Csn^{1/p})\Big\} - e^{-s^{-p}} \right|
     = o(1).
   $$

## Three-type theorem for surprisals

- Gaussian-like surprisal tails $\Rightarrow$ maximum surprisal is reversed Weibull
- Exponential surprisal tails $\Rightarrow$ maximum surprisal is Gumbel
- Only polynomial moments $\Rightarrow$ maximum surprisal is Fréchet

::: {.block}
[Corollary (via Pickands--Balkema--de Haan)]{.block-title}

The upper tail of the surprisal distribution can be approximated by a Generalized Pareto Distribution, [even if the assumed density $f$ is incorrect]{.alert}, provided one of A1--A3 is satisfied.
:::

## Approximate GPD surprisal probabilities

- $f^*$: the assumed (possibly incorrect) density.
  Compute $s_t = -\log f^*(y_t)$.
- $u$: the $(1 - \beta)$ sample quantile of $\{s_t\}$ (typically $\beta = 0.1$).
- Fit a GPD to the exceedances $s_t - u$, giving density $\hat{g}$ on $(u,\infty)$.
- For $s_t > u$: $\quad \hat{p}_t = \beta \int_{s_t}^\infty \hat{g}(s)\,ds$.
  For $s_t \le u$, set $\hat{p}_t = \beta$.

::: {.fragment}
- Only needs $f^*$ to get the *ordering* of the extreme surprisals approximately right.
- `surprisals_prob(..., approximation = "gpd")`
:::

## Univariate experiment

What happens when the distribution used to compute surprisals is mis-specified?

::: {.block}
[Data N(0,1)]{.block-title}

- 1000 observations from a N(0,1) distribution
- Surprisals computed using a t(4) distribution.
- Estimate surprisal probabilities using N(0,1), t(4), GPD

## Hampel identifier {.nostretch}

```{r}

#| out-width: "100%"

include_png(tar_read(fig_hampel_png))
```

::: {.columns}
::::: {.column .math-left width="54%"}
$$
  \begin{aligned}
    m_t & = \text{median}(y_{t-w}, \dots, y_{t+w})                 \\
    a_t & = \text{median}(|y_{t-w} - m_t|, \dots, |y_{t+w} - m_t|) \\
    e_t & = (y_t - m_t)/(a_t/0.6745)
  \end{aligned}
$$

- Anomaly if $|e_t| > k$
:::::
::::: {.column .fragment width="46%"}
- Implicit model: $y_t \sim \text{N}(m_t, \sigma_t^2)$ with $\sigma_t = a_t/0.6745$
- Better: surprisals of $e_t$ under N(0,1), with probabilities from a GPD
:::::
:::

## Surprisals from an STL decomposition {.small}

::: {.columns}
::::: {.column width="34%"}
Local medians fail with seasonality.

Replace by a better signal estimate.

- STL: $y_t = T_t + S_t + R_t$ (Cleveland et al., 1990; Bandara\ et al., 2025)
- $a_t$: robust estimate of $\{R_t\}$ stdev, separately for each age group
- $e_t = R_t / a_t$; surprisals under N(0,1), probabilities from GPD
:::::
::::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r}
#| label: stl-stmf
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

stmf_scores <- us_stmf |>
  model(stl = STL(Mortality)) |>
  augment() |>
  group_by(`Age group`) |>
  mutate(e = .resid / robustbase::s_Qn(.resid)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(prob = surprisals_prob(e, "gpd", distribution = dist_normal())) |>
  arrange(prob)
```

```{r}
#| label: stmf_scores_print

tar_read(stmf_scores_table)
```
:::::
:::

window.addEventListener("load", function () {

  var video = slide.querySelector(".zoom-video video");

    slide.classList.add("zoom-done");

    var prev = e.previousSlide && Reveal.getIndices(e.previousSlide).h;
    if (prev === Reveal.getIndices(slide).h - 1) {
      slide.classList.remove("zoom-done");
      video.currentTime = 0;
      video.play();
    } else {
      slide.classList.add("zoom-done");

  });
});

## Weird series {#part-weird-series .section-slide background-color="#0f2a44"}

`r section("Weird series")`

## Feature-based anomaly detection

- Comparing whole time series directly is awkward: different scales, lengths, and offsets.
- Summarise each series by a vector of [features]{.alert}: strength of trend and seasonality, autocorrelations, spectral entropy, level shifts, ...
- Each series becomes a point in $\mathbb{R}^d$.
  A weird series is a multivariate anomaly in feature space.
- Most features are scale-free, so series are flagged for their shape and dynamics, not their size.
- A series that is unusual in a way not captured by any feature will not be found.

## Kernel density surprisals {.small}

::: {.block}
[KDE]{.block-title}

$$
  \boldsymbol{y}_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^d, \quad \hat{f}(\boldsymbol{y})
  = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n |\boldsymbol{H}|^{-1/2} K\big(\boldsymbol{H}^{-1/2}(\boldsymbol{y} - \boldsymbol{y}_i)\big)
$$
:::

- $K$: spherically symmetric kernel; $\boldsymbol{H}$: $d \times d$ bandwidth matrix.
- Each observation inflates its own density estimate: use leave-one-out.

::: {.fragment}
::::: {.block}
[LOO KDE values]{.block-title}

$$
  \hat{f}_{-i}(\boldsymbol{y}_i)
  = \frac{1}{n - 1} \big( n \hat{f}(\boldsymbol{y}_i) - |\boldsymbol{H}|^{-1/2} K(\boldsymbol{0}) \big)
$$

- Surprisals $s_i = -\log \hat{f}_{-i}(\boldsymbol{y}_i)$; probabilities from the GPD.
:::::
:::

## Surveillance using forecast distributions

For each $t = I, I + 1, \dots$, and each series $i = 1,\dots,M$:

- Fit a model to $y_{i,1},\dots,y_{i,t}$ giving one-step forecast density $f_{i,t+1}(y \mid \mathcal{F}_{i,t})$
- Surprisal: $s_{i,t+1} = -\log f_{i,t+1}(y_{i,t+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_{i,t})$
- Surprisal probability: $p_{i,t+1} = \mathbb{P}(S \ge s_{i,t+1})$, where\
  $S = -\log f_{i,t+1}(Y \mid \mathcal{F}_{i,t})$ and $Y \sim f_{i,t+1}$
- Start at $I = 36$ (3 years), one-step ETS forecasts, rolling origin.

## Rolling origin one-step forecasts

```{r}
#| label: fig_tscv

include_png(tar_read(fig_tscv_png))
```

## Surveillance using forecast distributions

::: {.incremental}
- If $f_{i,t+1}$ is the true conditional density, and $G_{i,t+1}$ is continuous, then
  $$
    p_{i,t+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_{i,t} \sim \text{U}(0,1)
  $$
  so the $p_{i,t}$ are iid U(0,1) over $t$ (a PIT of the surprisals).
- Thresholding at $\alpha$ gives a false alarm rate of $\alpha$ per series per period.
- Model updated each period, so a level shift is flagged when it happens, then becomes the "new normal".
- ETS: Gaussian forecast distributions, so $p_{i,t+1}$ is a two-sided $z$-test on the one-step forecast error.
:::

## A first iteration: $t = 36$

```{r}
#| label: pbsfc
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

pbs_fc <- pbs |>
  filter(t <= 36) |>
  group_by_key() |>
  filter(cumsum(Scripts) > 0, n() >= 36) |>
  ungroup() |>
  model(ets = ETS(Scripts)) |>
  forecast(h = 1)
```

## Rolling forward through the data

```{r}
#| label: pbsloop
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

pbs$prob <- NA_real_
for (i in seq(36, max(pbs$t) - 1)) {
  pbs_fc <- pbs |>
    filter(t <= i) |>
    group_by_key() |>
    filter(cumsum(Scripts) > 0, n() >= 36) |>
    ungroup() |>
    model(ets = ETS(Scripts)) |>
    forecast(h = 1)
  # ... compute surprisals_prob() for time i+1 and store in pbs$prob
}
```

## Surveillance across several series {.small}

Some events affect many series at once: mildly unusual in each, very unusual together.

- $M_t$: number of series monitored at time $t$
- $N_t$: number of series with $p_{i,t} < 0.001$
- If series independent, each flagged with probability $\pi$:\
  $N_t \sim \text{Binomial}(M_t, \pi)$; compute $\mathbb{P}(N_t \ge n_t)$

::: {.fragment}
- If forecast densities were correct, $\pi = 0.001$.
- But ETS forecast distributions are too narrow: `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(pbs_scores$prob < 0.001, na.rm = TRUE))`% of observations have $p_{i,t} < 0.001$.
- So estimate $\pi$ in real time from all previous months.
:::

  Still useful for ranking months.

## Summary {#part-summary .section-slide background-color="#0f2a44"}

`r section("Summary")`

## Summary

- [Weird times]{.alert}: remove the signal (moving median, STL), then surprisals of standardised residuals.
  Check for artefacts near large anomalies.
- [Weird series]{.alert}: features $\rightarrow$ multivariate anomaly detection, using LOO KDE surprisals.
- [Surveillance]{.alert}: surprisals of one-step forecast densities, refitting as data arrive.
  Forecast distributions are often too narrow.
- In every case: surprisal = $-\log$(conditional density); extreme surprisals have an approximate GPD tail even when $f$ is wrong.

```{=html}
<script>
// On slides with class "code-steps", show the n-th ".step-output" block when n
// code-highlight steps have been revealed, so outputs follow the code
window.addEventListener("load", function () {
  function update() {
    document.querySelectorAll("section.code-steps").forEach(function (slide) {
      var step = slide.querySelectorAll("code.fragment.visible").length;
      slide.querySelectorAll(".step-output").forEach(function (out, i) {
        out.classList.toggle("current", i === step);
      });
    });
  }
  ["ready", "slidechanged", "fragmentshown", "fragmenthidden"].forEach(function (e) {
    Reveal.on(e, update);
  });
  update();
});
</script>
```
